assumptions: many small genetic effects across hundreds or thousands of variants
conclusion: Polygenicity compromises phenotype prediction from individual genetic profiles.
span: The polygenic model of human phenotypes has long been hypothesized, but only in recent years have the results from genome-wide association study (GWAS) revealed that much of the genetic basis for most complex traits comprises small effects of hundreds or even thousands of variants. For clinical outcomes, this polygenic effect can be considered a genetic liability to disease risk. While prediction of phenotype from an individual’s genetic profile is compromised by this polygenicity, the application of polygenic risk scores (PRS) has shown that prediction is sufficiently accurate for a number of applications.

assumptions: trait-associated variants and estimated effects are available
conclusion: A PRS is a genome-wide sum of an individual's genotypes weighted by estimated effects on the trait.
scope: Score definition; no Bayesian prior specified.
span: A PRS for an individual is a summation of their genotypes at variants genome-wide, weighted by effect sizes on a trait of interest.

objects: SNP P-values Pi; inclusion threshold PT
assumptions: base-phenotype GWAS association evidence is available
conclusion: A SNP enters the score when its base-GWAS P-value is below the chosen threshold, and scores are typically computed at multiple thresholds.
span: SNPs are generally selected for inclusion in a polygenic risk score based on the degree of evidence, according to P-value, for their association with the base phenotype in a GWAS – SNP i will be included in a PRS if Pi is smaller than a threshold, PT. PRS are typically calculated at a number of different P-value thresholds, PT.
location: prsice | journal OA version | Supplementary Note 1

assumptions: GWAS genotype effects are estimated using an additive model
conclusion: The described GWAS effect estimate assumes an additive effect per unit increase in genotype.
scope: Base-GWAS effect estimation; no general SNP independence assumption.
span: Under the usual additive assumption made in GWAS, a corresponding effect size is estimated, byβi, for the effect of a unit increase in genotype, Gij, on the phenotype.
location: prsice | journal OA version | Supplementary Note 1

assumptions: regression family is appropriate for the target phenotype data type
conclusion: Association is evaluated by regressing target phenotype on PRS, with linear regression given as the continuous-phenotype example.
scope: No general likelihood or prior specified.
span: PRS, which we see here are based on effect size estimates relating to the ‘base phenotype’, are calculated across all individuals giving n scores per threshold, PT. The association between these PRS and the target phenotype can then be evaluated in an appropriate regression model (depending on the data type of the target phenotype, eg. linear regression if the phenotype is continuous).
location: prsice | journal OA version | Supplementary Note 1

assumptions: PRS is used to test shared genetic aetiology between traits
conclusion: The described cross-trait analysis constructs base-phenotype scores in an independent target data set.
scope: Independence stated for this cross-trait design.
span: Here PRS on the base phenotype are calculated, using GWAS results, in individuals from an independent data set, and these are used as predictors of the target phenotype in a regression (see Supplementary Note S1).

assumptions: base and target phenotype may be the same
conclusion: The standard analysis takes base-phenotype GWAS results and target genotypes and produces individual scores and model-fit evaluations over thresholds.
span: It requires only GWAS results on a base phenotype and genotype data on a target phenotype as input (base and target phenotype may be the same); it outputs PRS for each individual and figures depicting the PRS model fit at a range of PT.
location: prsice | journal OA version | 2 Overview of PRSice

assumptions: minimum, maximum and spacing are chosen
conclusion: High-resolution scoring computes PRS on a large evenly spaced grid of P-value thresholds.
scope: Grid bounds and increments are settings.
span: High-resolution polygenic risk scoring, as performed in PRSice, calculates PRS at a large number of evenly spaced P-value thresholds, between a minimum and maximum bound.
location: prsice | journal OA version | Supplementary Note 3

assumptions: a finite high-resolution grid is tested
conclusion: Grid search approximates the best-fit PRS; the authors state that identifying the true best fit requires testing every possible threshold.
scope: Relative to exhaustive threshold search; no out-of-sample optimality guarantee.
span: This high-resolution approach enables us to identify the best-fit PRS to a high degree of approximation; the true best-fit PRS can only be identified by testing PRS at every possible PT, but we instead test them at high-resolution in order to reduce total computational time substantially with negligible loss in accuracy.
location: prsice | journal OA version | Supplementary Note 3

objects: LD clumping; discovery P-value; target LD
assumptions: illustrated analysis uses 250 kb windows and pairwise r-squared below 0.1
conclusion: The illustrated clumping selects the lowest-discovery-P-value SNP in a sliding window and retains variants satisfying a target-data LD threshold.
span: Linkage disequilibrium (LD) was accounted for by selecting the SNP in the base phenotype data set with the lowest discovery P-value in a sliding window of 250kb, only retaining variants with a pairwise LD r2 < 0.1, according to LD calculated in the target data set.
location: prsice | journal OA version | Supplementary Note 2

objects: best-fit PRS association P-value; multiple tests
conclusion: Selecting the best-fit score entails multiple tests and inflates its unadjusted association significance.
scope: Inference after threshold search requires adjustment.
span: Under high-resolution PRS in particular, multiple tests are performed and so the P-value of the best-fit PRS will be inflated.

assumptions: each successive threshold adds few SNPs and many SNPs are already included
conclusion: The authors argue that correlated threshold-specific tests make Bonferroni correction by the number of tests overly conservative.
span: Under high-resolution a small number of SNPs are added to the model at each new P-value threshold. Thus, the resulting PRS is likely to be very similar to the previous, especially once a large number of SNPs are already included, so there is high correlation between the multiple tests performed. Therefore, a simple Bonferroni correction or similar for the number of tests performed will produce an overly conservative adjustment for the multiple testing.
location: prsice | journal OA version | Supplementary Note 4

assumptions: chromosome-19 SCZ/MDD permutation studies with clumping, two ancestry PCs and target sample sizes 1000, 2000 and 3000
conclusion: The permutation results support a 0.004 threshold for a false-positive rate below 0.05 in the studied design; the authors provisionally recommend 0.001.
scope: Empirical calibration; a more extensive study is needed for a reliable general threshold.
span: These results indicated that an alpha threshold of 0.004 must be applied to high-resolution best- fit PRS in order to ensure a false-positive rate below 0.05 (table S1). Prior to an extensive study to estimate a more reliable significance threshold for high-resolution PRS, we suggest a more conservative significance threshold of P = 0.001.
location: prsice | journal OA version | Supplementary Note 4

objects: cross-trait PRS regression; earlier ISC analysis
assumptions: target phenotype is predicted from base-trait PRS in independent data
conclusion: The paper attributes the first application of the described cross-trait PRS technique to the International Schizophrenia Consortium (2009).
scope: Historical relation to the earlier cross-trait PRS analysis.
span: This technique was first applied by the International Schizophrenia Consortium (2009), demonstrating that genetic risk for schizophrenia (SCZ) is a predictor of bipolar disorder.
